title: Gospel of Mark
intro: 40 days through the Gospel of Mark, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, the books that tell the story of Jesus' life. Many scholars think it was the first one written, around 65 to 70 AD. "Gospel" means "good news," and Mark states his whole point in his very first line: who he believes Jesus is. Starting today, 40 days through Mark, one verse at a time.

Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan River, and Mark describes a voice from heaven saying these words. This is where Jesus' public work begins. The line echoes Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42 from the Hebrew scriptures, which Mark's first readers would have recognized.

Jesus' first words in Mark, and a summary of his whole message. "Repent" translates the Greek word metanoia, which literally means a change of mind or direction, not just feeling sorry. The "kingdom of God" is the central theme of his teaching.

Simon (later called Peter) and his brother Andrew were fishermen on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus calls them with a play on their own trade, and Mark says they left their nets right away. His first followers were ordinary working people.

The day before, Jesus had been healing crowds in the town of Capernaum late into the night. The next morning he gets up before dawn to be alone and pray. Mark shows this pattern more than once: busy public days balanced with quiet time away.

Four friends can't get through the crowd, so they dig through the roof and lower their paralyzed friend down to Jesus. Notice whose faith Jesus responds to: the friends'. The religious teachers watching are shocked that he claims to forgive sins, something they believed only God could do.

Jesus is criticized for eating with tax collectors and "sinners," people treated as outsiders. Tax collectors worked for Rome and were often seen as traitors and cheats. His answer is a simple analogy: a doctor goes where the sick people are.

posts.display: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”
posts.caption: The Sabbath is the weekly day of rest from the Ten Commandments. Jesus' disciples were criticized for picking grain to eat on it. His point: the day of rest was given as a gift to serve people, not as a burden people exist to serve.

Some critics claim Jesus drives out demons by the power of Satan. He answers with logic: a house fighting against itself would collapse, so the accusation makes no sense. Abraham Lincoln borrowed this line for his famous 1858 "House Divided" speech about slavery.

The end of the Parable of the Sower. A farmer scatters seed that lands on a path, on rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil. Jesus explains that the soils are different ways people receive his message, and only the good soil produces a lasting crop. A hundredfold harvest would have sounded almost impossible to a farmer.

posts.display: “To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it? It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth. But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants.”
posts.caption: Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed, proverbial for being tiny. The image is about small, unimpressive beginnings that grow far beyond what anyone would expect. He adds that the plant puts out branches big enough for birds to nest in its shade, which many scholars hear as an echo of great trees standing for kingdoms in Ezekiel and Daniel.

A storm hits the disciples' boat on the Sea of Galilee while Jesus sleeps. Several of them were experienced fishermen, and they are terrified. In the Hebrew scriptures, calming the sea is something only God does (see Psalm 107), which is why the next verse matters so much.

The disciples' reaction after the storm stops. They are more afraid now than during the storm. This question, "Who is this?", runs through the whole first half of Mark and finally gets answered in chapter 8.

A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak in a crowd, hoping to be healed without anyone noticing. Under the purity customs of the time, her condition would have kept her isolated. Jesus stops, finds her, and calls her "Daughter," restoring her in public as well as in body.

Jairus, a synagogue leader, had begged Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way, messengers arrive to say she has died. This is what Jesus tells him in that moment. The story ends with Jesus raising the girl back to life.

Jesus returns to his hometown of Nazareth, and the people who watched him grow up can't accept him. "Isn't this the carpenter?" they ask. Mark notes that he did few miracles there because of their unbelief.

The disciples have just returned from their first mission, so busy they haven't even had time to eat. Jesus invites them to get away and rest. Even with crowds waiting, rest is something he makes room for.

The crowds follow them anyway, and Jesus responds with compassion instead of frustration. "Sheep without a shepherd" is an image from the Hebrew scriptures for people without good leaders. What comes next is the feeding of the five thousand.

Religious leaders criticize the disciples for eating without ritual handwashing. Jesus moves the focus from outward rules to the heart. A few verses later he explains what he means: things like greed, deceit, envy, and arrogance are what truly make a person unclean.

The turning point of Mark. After all the "Who is this?" moments, Jesus asks his disciples directly. Peter's answer, "the Christ," is the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning "anointed one": the promised king Israel had been waiting for.

Right after Peter's answer, Jesus tells them he will suffer and die, and Peter objects. Then Jesus says this to everyone. In the Roman world, crucifixion was a public execution, and carrying your cross meant walking to your own death. It was a shocking image, not a decorative one.
This continues yesterday's verse. The Greek word translated "soul" here, psyche, can also mean "life." Jesus contrasts gaining everything the world offers with losing the self that matters most.

A father brings his son, who suffers violent seizures, to Jesus for help. When Jesus tells him that everything is possible for someone who believes, the father answers with this honest admission. Many readers find this verse comforting because it shows belief and doubt existing in the same person.
On the road, the disciples had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. Jesus sits them down and flips their idea of status: in his view, greatness comes through serving others.

People bring their children to Jesus, and the disciples try to send them away. Children had little social status in that culture. Mark says Jesus was indignant, a strong word, and that he took the children in his arms and blessed them.

A rich man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus tells him to sell what he owns and give to the poor, and the man walks away sad. The camel and needle image is deliberate exaggeration. The disciples were stunned, because wealth was often seen as a sign of God's favor.
After the camel line, the disciples ask, "Then who can be saved?" This is Jesus' answer: salvation is not something people can achieve on their own, but God can do what people can't.

James and John ask for the seats of honor next to Jesus. He answers that his followers should serve, just as he came to serve. A "ransom" was a price paid to free a captive or a slave. Many readers see this as the key verse explaining why, in Mark's telling, Jesus goes to his death.
Jesus connects prayer with forgiveness: before asking God for anything, let go of what you are holding against other people. The same idea shows up in the Lord's Prayer in Matthew and Luke.

Opponents try to trap Jesus: should Jews pay taxes to Rome? Saying yes would anger the crowd, and saying no would sound like rebellion. He asks for a coin, points to Caesar's image on it, and gives this answer. The hidden second half: if the coin bears Caesar's image, people bear God's image (Genesis 1:27).

posts.display: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.”
posts.caption: A teacher of the law asks Jesus which commandment is the most important. Jesus answers by quoting two passages from the Torah, Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Putting love of God and love of neighbor together as the summary of everything became central to Christian teaching.

Jesus watches people put money into the temple treasury. The rich give large amounts, and a poor widow gives two small copper coins, worth almost nothing. Jesus measures the gift by what it cost her, not by its size.

Chapter 13 is Jesus' long talk about the coming destruction of the temple in Jerusalem and the end of the age. (Rome destroyed the temple in 70 AD.) He closes with this contrast between what fades and what lasts.

The Last Supper: a Passover meal Jesus shares with his disciples the night before he dies. Passover remembers Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt. Jesus gives the bread a new meaning, and this moment is the origin of communion, which Christians still practice today.

Jesus prays in the garden of Gethsemane, deeply distressed, knowing what is coming. "Abba" is the Aramaic word for father, a close family word. The "cup" is an image for suffering. He asks to be spared, then surrenders to God's will.

Three times Jesus comes back from praying and finds his closest friends asleep. This is his warning to them. "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak" became a common English saying because of this verse.

Jesus' last words in Mark, spoken in Aramaic from the cross. They are the first line of Psalm 22, a psalm that opens in anguish and ends in trust. Mark keeps the original language here, one of only a few places he does.

A Roman centurion, an army officer over roughly 80 soldiers, watches Jesus die. He becomes the first person in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God, which brings the story full circle back to the very first verse of the book.

Early Sunday morning, women who had followed Jesus come to the tomb to anoint his body with spices. The stone has been rolled away, and a young man dressed in white tells them this. The resurrection is the foundation of the Christian faith.

The risen Jesus sends out his eleven remaining disciples with these words, from Mark's longer ending (16:9 to 20). The oldest surviving manuscripts stop at verse 8, with the women fleeing the empty tomb in fear, so most scholars think these verses were added later; many churches still read them as Scripture. That's the whole Gospel of Mark. Thank you for reading it with me.
